The Confused Patient

A systematic, case-based approach to delirium, encephalopathy, dementia, and their neurologic mimics — from a neurologist's perspective.
Alexandra Filippakis, D.O.  ·  Greenleaf Neurology, PLLC  ·  Notes built from slides + live lecture transcript
01

Foundations: Naming the Problem

Neurologists love their terminology — we have our own language and we're very specific about what we call things. "Confusion" is the title of this talk, but it's not a word we actually use once we're at the bedside.

Case 1

A 72-year-old woman is postoperative day 2 after hip arthroplasty. The nurse reports she has been "talking to the wall," intermittently drowsy, then agitated and pulling at her IV lines. Medications: oxycodone 5 mg q4h PRN, ondansetron, cefazolin.

Question: Is this delirium, dementia, a stroke, or something else? How would you approach this patient at the bedside?

"Confusion" Is Not a Diagnosis — It's a Symptom

If a learner tells Dr. Filippakis a patient is "confused," she isn't satisfied — that word is too vague for how neurology actually communicates about mental status. Four terms carry the real information:

⚡
Delirium
Acute, fluctuating
Disturbance of attention & awareness with an identifiable underlying medical cause.
🧠
Encephalopathy
Pathophysiologic state
Brain dysfunction ranging from subclinical to coma — often used interchangeably with delirium.
📉
Dementia
Chronic, progressive
A neurodegenerative process — months to years, not hours to days.
🎭
Psychosis
Primary psychiatric
Attention is preserved, at least early on.
Board Pearl
Delirium is the clinical phenotype; encephalopathy is the pathophysiologic process — the two overlap constantly but are not synonyms. You can absolutely have a patient with both dementia and delirium at once.

Anatomy of Consciousness

Consciousness has two components, and where a lesion sits determines which one it hits:

Arousal (Level)

The Ascending Reticular Activating System (ARAS) — starts in the brainstem, relays through the thalamus, projects to the cortex.

Brainstem→ Thalamus→ Cortex

Damage here → decreased level of consciousness.

Awareness (Content)

Distributed cortical networks — attention, language, memory, executive function.

Damage here → the patient is confused/encephalopathic but stays awake, as long as the ARAS itself is untouched.

Board Pearl
Focal lesions causing disorders of consciousness typically involve bilateral hemispheres, the dominant hemisphere (a large left-sided lesion can mimic confusion via fluent aphasia), or the thalamus/brainstem (ARAS disruption).

DSM-5 Criteria for Delirium

  1. Disturbance in attention and awareness
  2. Develops over hours to days; fluctuates in severity — this is the rule, not the exception
  3. Additional cognitive disturbance (memory, orientation, language, perception)
  4. Not better explained by a pre-existing neurocognitive disorder (i.e. dementia)
  5. Evidence of an underlying medical cause
Key Concept
Delirium is always secondary — it doesn't happen randomly. When you see it, put on your investigator hat and find the cause.

The Confusion Assessment Method (CAM)

Sensitivity 94–100%, specificity 90–95% — the most widely used bedside screening tool. Diagnosis requires Feature 1 + Feature 2 + (Feature 3 OR Feature 4):

#FeatureNotes
1Acute onset and fluctuating courseAsk a knowledgeable informant about baseline
2InattentionTHE cardinal feature
3Disorganized thinkingRambling, illogical, unpredictable
4Altered level of consciousnessAnything besides "alert"
"I'll tell you the truth — in neurology, we don't really use the CAM. It's sort of embedded in the way that we think about the patient, but we don't actively go through a checklist. Nurses do that, and it is helpful. What we do is testing attention at the bedside as part of the observation on rounds."

Testing Attention at the Bedside

  • Digit span forward (normal ≥5 digits)
  • Days of the week backward
  • Months of the year backward
  • Spell WORLD backward
  • Serial 7s (100, 93, 86, 79…)

If the patient can't sustain attention on any of these — customize down to something as simple as "count down from 20" if needed — inattention is present.

Terminology Note
When neurology says "inattentive," it does not mean ADHD-type inattention. It means an acquired inability to focus and track a conversation — a very different clinical phenomenon.

Delirium Subtypes

SubtypePrevalencePresentationDetection
Hyperactive~25%Agitation, hallucinations, pulling at linesEasily recognized
Hypoactive~50%Withdrawn, drowsy, quietMost often missed
Mixed~25%Fluctuates between bothVariable
Board Pearl
Hypoactive delirium is the most common subtype in older adults, the most frequently missed, and carries the highest mortality.

The Inouye Model — Vulnerability + Insult

Predisposing Factors (Vulnerability)

  • Advanced age
  • Dementia / MCI
  • Sensory impairment
  • Functional dependence
  • Comorbidity burden

Precipitating Factors (Insults)

  • Medications
  • Infection
  • Surgery
  • Metabolic derangement
  • Immobilization, sleep deprivation
HIGH vulnerability+ MINOR insult= Delirium e.g. elderly patient with MCI + one new anticholinergic
LOW vulnerability+ MAJOR insult= Delirium e.g. young healthy patient + ICU stay after major surgery
POLL 1
A 72-year-old woman is POD#2 after hip arthroplasty. Using the CAM, which feature is REQUIRED for the diagnosis of delirium?
Inattention is the cardinal feature of delirium and Feature 2 of the CAM — it must always be present alongside acute/fluctuating onset (Feature 1), plus either disorganized thinking or altered consciousness.
02

The Delirium Differential

Once you know it's delirium, the real work starts: finding the underlying cause. Most causes in older adults have nothing to do with the brain itself.

"I WATCH DEATH"

I – W – A – T – C – H

  • I — Infection
  • W — Withdrawal (alcohol, benzodiazepines)
  • A — Acute metabolic (electrolytes, glucose, renal, hepatic)
  • T — Trauma (falls, subdural hematoma)
  • C — CNS pathology (stroke, seizure, tumor, hydrocephalus)
  • H — Hypoxia

D – E – A – T – H

  • D — Deficiencies (thiamine, B12)
  • E — Endocrinopathies (thyroid, adrenal)
  • A — Acute vascular (stroke, MI, PE)
  • T — Toxins/drugs (#1 reversible cause)
  • H — Heavy metals
Key Concept
Most causes of delirium in older adults lie OUTSIDE the brain. Yes, sometimes it's a stroke or a tumor — but usually it's an infection, a medication change, a vitamin deficiency, hypoxia, or a metabolic derangement.

Medications — the BEERS List

High-risk drug classes to always screen for on medication reconciliation:

  • Anticholinergics — oxybutynin (very common overactive-bladder drug), diphenhydramine, TCAs
  • Benzodiazepines — especially long-acting (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide)
  • Opioids — especially in the opioid-naive elderly (think post-op ortho)
  • Fluoroquinolones — they cross the blood-brain barrier
  • Corticosteroids — dose-dependent; high-dose IV methylprednisolone is a real offender
Board Pearl — Anticholinergic Toxidrome
"Hot as a hare, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter."
"Always, always, always do a thorough medication reconciliation, including OTC and supplements. A lot of times your job as the 3rd- or 4th-year student is to find a family member — or call the patient's pharmacy directly — and confirm what was actually dispensed. It's actually an honor when we ask you to do that."

Metabolic Derangements

CauseKey Clinical FeatureBoard Pearl
HyponatremiaConfusion → seizures → comaCorrect slowly (<8 mEq/L/day) or risk osmotic demyelination
Hypercalcemia"Stones, bones, groans, psychiatric moans"—
Hepatic encephalopathyAsterixis (negative myoclonus)Triphasic waves on EEG
UremiaMyoclonus, asterixis—
HypoglycemiaDiaphoresis, tremor, confusionAlways check glucose
HypercapniaSomnolence, headacheCO2 retention in COPD
Case 2

A 55-year-old man is found down, confused, with horizontal nystagmus and a wide-based, ataxic gait. Glucose is 60 mg/dL.

Wernicke Encephalopathy — The Malnourished Alcoholic

The classic triad — present in only ~10% of cases: (1) confusion, (2) oculomotor dysfunction (nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia), (3) gait ataxia. Not just alcoholism — also seen with hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery, malignancy, anorexia nervosa.

Anatomy & Imaging Pathology targets: mammillary bodies (most characteristic), periaqueductal gray, medial thalamus, floor of the 4th ventricle. A/B = CT; C–E = MRI showing symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in periventricular regions. The Confused Patient, Filippakis
Board Pearl
Bilateral hippocampal signal = HSV encephalitis, NOT Wernicke's.
Critical Management Pearl
THIAMINE BEFORE GLUCOSE — always. Glucose metabolism consumes thiamine, so giving dextrose to a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's. Order of operations: (1) IV thiamine (500 mg IV TID × 3 days), THEN (2) IV dextrose for hypoglycemia. Untreated Wernicke's → Korsakoff syndrome (irreversible anterograde amnesia with confabulation).
"There's no harm in giving someone IV thiamine — you're not going to overdose them on it. I remember rounding at Tufts with an attending who'd be very upset at Morning Report if we hadn't given thiamine to every confused patient overnight. You give it empirically; you don't wait for the level to result."
POLL 2
A 55-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is found down. He is confused with nystagmus and ataxia. Glucose is 60 mg/dL. What is the MOST appropriate FIRST step?
Thiamine is given empirically before glucose — there's no harm even if the patient isn't deficient. Practically: IV thiamine is hanging before the patient is even registered and wheeled to CT, since labs are drawn and the "banana bag" is readily available in the ED.

Alcohol Withdrawal Timeline

Time After Last DrinkManifestation
6–24 hoursTremor, anxiety, insomnia, tachycardia
12–48 hoursSeizures (generalized tonic-clonic)
48–96 hoursDelirium tremens
Board Pearl
Delirium tremens = hyperactive delirium + autonomic instability + visual hallucinations. Mortality 5–15% if untreated. Treatment is benzodiazepines — this is the one exception to "avoid benzos in delirium."

Serotonin Syndrome vs. Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

FeatureSerotonin SyndromeNMS
OnsetHours (rapid)Days to weeks (slow)
Causative agentSerotonergic drugs (SSRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, ondansetron)Dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide)
NeuromuscularClonus, hyperreflexia, tremorLead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia
AutonomicHyperthermia, diaphoresis, diarrheaHyperthermia, diaphoresis
PupilsMydriasisNormal
TreatmentCyproheptadine + coolingDantrolene + bromocriptine + cooling
Board Pearl
Clonus = serotonin syndrome. Rigidity = NMS.
03

Neurologic Emergencies Mimicking Confusion

These are the diagnoses you cannot afford to miss — because "just delirium" is the wrong answer, and the treatment window is often narrow.

Case 3

A 68-year-old man's family says he has been "not making sense" for 3 hours. On exam he has fluent speech with nonsensical words and neologisms, poor comprehension, and NO hemiparesis.

The "Confused" Aphasic

Wernicke aphasia (left MCA stroke): fluent but meaningless speech, impaired comprehension — often with no motor deficit, which is exactly why it gets mistaken for confusion or psychosis.

"Think about the localization — Broca's area is right next to primary motor cortex, so a Broca's stroke almost always comes with weakness. Wernicke's area sits further back, so you're not hitting motor fibers at all. That's why a fluent aphasia can walk in looking like nothing more than 'confusion.'"
  • Right MCA stroke → hemineglect, anosognosia
  • Bilateral thalamic infarcts → acute confusion/coma
  • Posterior circulation stroke → vertigo, ataxia, altered consciousness
Board Pearl
Confusion (encephalopathy) + any focal neurologic finding = urgent neuroimaging. CT is the fastest, most available first test.
POLL 3
A 68-year-old man is brought in for "not making sense" for 3 hours. He speaks fluently but uses nonsensical words. He does not follow commands. No hemiparesis. Most likely diagnosis?
Fluent, meaningless speech with impaired comprehension and no weakness is the classic left-MCA-inferior-division Wernicke aphasia — a focal stroke masquerading as "confusion."
Case 4

An 80-year-old woman had a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure 4 hours ago. She received IV lorazepam and convulsions stopped. She remains obtunded with subtle, rhythmic eye twitching.

The Elderly Patient Who Won't Wake Up — NCSE

Nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) is prolonged seizure activity without overt convulsions. Almost 48% of patients treated for convulsive status epilepticus continue to have electrographic seizures. Presents as persistent altered mental status, staring, subtle automatisms, abnormal eye movements.

"When you see the word 'rhythmic' in a neurology vignette, that's the exam trying to tell you something about seizure activity — rhythmic eye twitching, rhythmic movements, rhythmic EEG discharges. Train yourself to catch that word."

Salzburg Consensus Criteria for NCSE

Diagnosis requires EEG showing one of:

  • Epileptiform discharges >2.5/second, OR
  • Slower discharges with spatiotemporal evolution, OR
  • Slower discharges with a clinical correlate, OR
  • Response to IV antiseizure medication (benzodiazepine trial)
Board Pearl
Spatiotemporal evolution is the key feature distinguishing NCSE from the triphasic waves of metabolic encephalopathy. Any patient with unexplained persistent AMS, especially after a treated seizure → order continuous EEG.

CNS Infectious / Inflammatory Processes

InfectionKey FeaturesBoard Pearl
Bacterial meningitisFever, headache, nuchal rigidity, AMSDo NOT delay antibiotics for imaging
HSV encephalitisSeizures, personality change, without feverTemporal lobe predilection; empiric acyclovir
Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitisPsychiatric → seizures → movement disorder → autonomic instabilityYoung women; check for ovarian teratoma
Case 5

A 24-year-old woman has a 2-week history of personality change, progressing to paranoia, then seizures, then orofacial dyskinesias. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. MRI brain is NORMAL (normal in up to 50% of cases).

The Young Woman with Bizarre Behavior — Anti-NMDA Receptor Encephalitis

Diagnostic test: CSF anti-NMDA receptor antibodies. Association: ovarian teratoma — always obtain pelvic imaging.

Clinical Staging

  1. Psychiatric symptoms (often initially misdiagnosed)
  2. Seizures
  3. Movement disorders (orofacial dyskinesias, choreoathetosis)
  4. Autonomic instability
  5. Decreased consciousness
"I had a patient as a junior resident in the neuro ICU at Tufts — a young woman, I still remember her name, Shakira. She was in the ICU for months. Constantly having non-convulsive status, autonomic storms where her blood pressure and heart rate would shoot through the roof. She'd had two psychiatric hospitalizations before anyone caught the seizure that got her to us. We threw everything at her — rituximab, steroids, plasma exchange. Unfortunately she died. It's one of those cases that just sticks with you. There's a book, Brain on Fire, about a woman who had this and survived — worth a listen if you ever get an audiobook window."

Structural Lesions

🩸
Subdural Hematoma
Elderly, anticoagulated, history of falls; may be chronic/subacute
⚡
Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
"Thunderclap headache" + confusion; often ruptured aneurysm
🎗️
Tumor / Metastasis
Subacute onset, focal deficits, headache
💧
Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus
Triad of gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, dementia — "wet, wobbly, wacky"
04

Distinguishing the Syndromes

Delirium vs. dementia vs. psychosis is the single highest-yield distinction in this entire lecture — worth drilling until it's automatic.

FeatureDeliriumDementiaPsychosis
OnsetAcute (hours–days)Insidious (months–years)Variable
CourseFluctuatingProgressiveStable within episodes
AttentionImpaired earlyPreserved until lateUsually preserved
ConsciousnessAltered (up or down)Normal until lateNormal
HallucinationsVisualLess common until lateAuditory
ReversibilityUsually reversibleGenerally irreversibleTreatable
EEGDiffuse slowingNormal or mild slowingNormal
Board Pearl
Visual hallucinations → delirium or Lewy body dementia. Auditory hallucinations → primary psychosis. Delirium superimposed on dementia occurs in ~50% of hospitalized dementia patients.
"I'd argue that number is closer to 90% in practice — patients with dementia already have that underlying vulnerability, so almost anything that lands them in the hospital is enough to push them into delirium on top."
POLL 4
Which clinical feature BEST distinguishes delirium from dementia?
Acute onset, fluctuating course, and inattention are the three features that define delirium and separate it from dementia's slow, steady decline.

Systematic Diagnostic Workup

History

  • Establish BASELINE mental status from a knowledgeable informant
  • Timeline: gradual or acute onset?
  • Complete medication review (incl. OTC, supplements, alcohol, recreational drugs)

Physical & Neuro Exam

  • Vitals including SpO2 and temperature
  • Attention testing (digit span, days backward)
  • Cranial nerves, motor/sensory, reflexes
  • Look for asterixis, myoclonus, meningismus, focal deficits

Labs

Routine: CBC, BMP, UA. Frequently helpful: LFTs, TSH, calcium, CXR, ECG, blood cultures. Selective: toxicology screen, ammonia, ABG, RPR, B12/folate, cortisol.

Board Pearl
Do NOT anchor on a positive UA in an elderly patient — asymptomatic bacteriuria is common and may not be the cause. This is a classic board "red herring."

Imaging, LP, and EEG

  • CT head: first-line (trauma, focal deficits, anticoagulation, no clear cause)
  • MRI brain: superior for stroke, encephalitis, demyelination
  • LP: if meningitis suspected; also for encephalitis, SAH
  • EEG: for suspected NCSE or to confirm organic brain dysfunction

Physical Exam Findings → Diagnosis

FindingThink...
Focal neurologic deficitStroke → neuroimaging
MeningismusMeningitis → LP
AsterixisHepatic or uremic encephalopathy
MyoclonusMetabolic, CJD, or NCSE
Nystagmus + ataxiaWernicke encephalopathy
Orofacial dyskinesiasAnti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
Clonus + hyperreflexiaSerotonin syndrome
Lead-pipe rigidityNMS
05

Management

Step 1 — Identify & Treat Cause

  • Correct metabolic derangements
  • Treat infections
  • Discontinue offending medications
  • Reverse hypoxia

Step 2 — Nonpharmacologic (First-Line)

  • Reorientation (clocks, calendars, familiar objects)
  • Sleep hygiene (minimize nighttime interruptions)
  • Early mobilization
  • Correct sensory deficits (glasses, hearing aids)
  • Avoid restraints (worsen agitation and delirium)
Board Pearl
The Hospital Elder Life Program (HELP) reduces delirium incidence by 30–40%. Simple orders like "shades up, lights on during the day; dark at night" reinforce circadian rhythm and genuinely move outcomes.
"This is where you'll butt heads with nursing staff — they've got vitals and neuro checks to do every four hours, and you're asking them to minimize nighttime interruptions. It takes more effort from everyone, but it's what's actually best for the patient. When you get paged at 2 a.m. for 'please just give Haldol to bed seven,' call first and ask what's actually going on before reaching for a prescription pad."

Pharmacologic Management — Last Resort

  • No FDA-approved medication for delirium
  • Antipsychotics (haloperidol, quetiapine) ONLY for severe agitation threatening patient/staff safety
  • Use lowest dose, shortest duration
  • Avoid benzodiazepines for delirium (worsen confusion) — EXCEPTION: alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal
  • Dexmedetomidine: emerging role in ICU delirium
06

EEG in the Confused Patient

The 3-Step Framework

  1. Background — is the background rhythm normal or slow?
  2. Superimposed activity — epileptiform discharges? Periodic discharges? Evolving rhythmic patterns?
  3. Clinical correlation — does the pattern match the clinical picture? (The same pattern can mean different things in different contexts.)

EEG Frequency Bands

BandFrequencyClinical Significance
Beta13–30 HzAwake, alert (also medications, anxiety)
Alpha8–13 HzAwake, eyes closed; the normal PDR, maximal occipital
Theta4–7 HzDrowsiness/light sleep; pathologic if diffuse in an awake adult
Delta0.5–4 HzDeep sleep; pathologic if present in an awake adult
Key Concept
Pathologic slowing = the EEG continuum shifts toward slower frequencies → indicates cortical dysfunction.

Delirium on EEG

Delirium — EEG 72F, POD#2, fluctuating drowsiness, visual hallucinations. Diffuse, disorganized background; generalized theta-range slowing (5–6 Hz); no epileptiform discharges. Consistent with delirium — severity of slowing correlates with delirium severity and predicts worse outcomes. The Confused Patient, Filippakis
Board Pearl
A normal EEG in a "confused" patient → reconsider a psychiatric disorder.

High-Yield EEG Patterns

PatternClassic AssociationKey Feature
Diffuse theta/delta slowingDelirium / metabolic encephalopathyNonspecific; severity correlates with depth
Triphasic wavesHepatic encephalopathyFrontally predominant, A-P lag, reactive
3 Hz spike-and-waveChildhood absence epilepsyBilateral, synchronous, abrupt onset/offset
Evolving epileptiform dischargesNCSESpatiotemporal evolution
Extreme delta brushAnti-NMDA receptor encephalitisBeta riding on delta waves
~1 Hz PSWCsCreutzfeldt-Jakob diseaseRegular periodicity; late-stage
Focal spikes/sharp wavesFocal epilepsyLateralized
Electrocerebral inactivityBrain death (ancillary)No activity ≥2 µV over 30 min

Triphasic Waves vs. NCSE

FeatureTriphasic WavesNCSE
MorphologyStable, stereotypedEvolving (changing frequency/morphology)
ReactivityReactive to stimulationMay not react
Phase lagAnterior-to-posteriorVariable
Clinical contextMetabolic (hepatic, uremic)Post-seizure, acute brain injury
When In Doubt
Benzodiazepine trial with concurrent EEG monitoring — if the discharges resolve within a minute of IV Ativan, that confirms ongoing seizure activity.
Triphasic Waves Classic 3-phase notched morphology (down–up–down) seen in metabolic (hepatic/uremic) encephalopathy — stable and stereotyped across the tracing. The Confused Patient, Filippakis
Nonconvulsive Status Epilepticus Rhythmic, periodic discharges (~4 Hz) that build up and evolve over the tracing — the spatiotemporal evolution that distinguishes NCSE from triphasic waves. The Confused Patient, Filippakis
POLL 5
What is the single most important EEG feature that distinguishes NCSE from triphasic waves?
NCSE discharges evolve in frequency and morphology over the tracing; triphasic waves stay stable and stereotyped throughout.

Extreme Delta Brush

Extreme Delta Brush Clinical context: 24F, personality change → seizures → orofacial dyskinesias. Diffuse delta slowing with rhythmic beta activity "riding" on delta waves — highly suggestive of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. Seen in ~30% of cases; resembles the normal delta brush of premature neonates. Correlates with longer hospitalization and worse short-term outcomes. The Confused Patient, Filippakis

Periodic Sharp-Wave Complexes (PSWCs)

Periodic Sharp-Wave Complexes Clinical context: 67M, rapidly progressive dementia over 8 weeks, myoclonus, ataxia. Severe diffuse slowing with periodic sharp-wave complexes at ~1 Hz — classic for Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Sensitivity ~64%, specificity ~91%; a late-stage finding — early CJD may show only nonspecific slowing. NOT pathognomonic — also seen in anoxic encephalopathy, lithium toxicity. Diagnostic standard now: PSWCs + DWI cortical ribboning + CSF RT-QuIC. The Confused Patient, Filippakis
ARS POLL 6
A 67-year-old man with rapidly progressive dementia has PSWCs at 1 Hz on EEG. Which test is MOST specific for confirming the diagnosis?
RT-QuIC (real-time quaking-induced conversion) of CSF is the most specific confirmatory test for prion disease — more specific than 14-3-3, which is a nonspecific marker of neuronal injury.
07

Case-Based Synthesis

Back to every case from the lecture — now with the diagnosis and management attached.

Case 1 Revisited — Multifactorial Delirium

72F, POD#2. Workup reveals: new oxycodone (opioid), a Foley catheter (immobilization, discomfort), sleep deprivation (nighttime vitals, noise), and no focal neurologic deficits.

Diagnosis: Multifactorial delirium (opioids + immobilization + sleep disruption).

Management: Reduce/discontinue oxycodone → multimodal analgesia (acetaminophen, ice). Remove Foley if possible; sleep protocol, reorientation, early mobilization. Avoid restraints, avoid benzodiazepines.

"It's actually become standard now for older orthopedic patients to not even get opioids as part of the routine post-op plan unless they're in real pain — multimodal analgesia first."

The "Confused" Aphasic — Wernicke Aphasia

Diagnosis: Wernicke aphasia — LEFT MCA STROKE. This is NOT delirium — it is a focal neurologic deficit, and the most commonly misidentified stroke presentation. Time-sensitive: is this patient within the thrombolysis/thrombectomy window? Always test language systematically: fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming.

The Malnourished Alcoholic — Wernicke Encephalopathy

Thiamine BEFORE glucose — always. Full triad present in only 10%. MRI: mammillary bodies, periaqueductal gray, medial thalamus. Untreated → Korsakoff syndrome (irreversible).

The Elderly Patient Who Won't Wake Up — NCSE

Continuous EEG is essential — clinical exam alone is insufficient. ~48% of treated convulsive SE patients have ongoing electrographic seizures. Salzburg criteria: discharges >2.5/s or slower with evolution. Treatment: IV benzodiazepine → resolution confirms diagnosis.

The Young Woman with Bizarre Behavior — Anti-NMDA Receptor Encephalitis

CSF anti-NMDA receptor antibodies = diagnostic test of choice. MRI normal in up to 50%. EEG may show extreme delta brush (~30%). Check for ovarian teratoma (pelvic imaging). Treatment: immunotherapy (IVIG, steroids, rituximab, plasma exchange).

Case 6 — Outpatient

A 78-year-old man is brought to his PCP by his daughter for 3 days of drowsiness, inattention, and calling her by his deceased wife's name. PMH: mild cognitive impairment, hypertension, BPH. 5 days ago, urgent care started oxybutynin for urinary frequency. Exam: drowsy, inattentive, no focal deficits, dry mucous membranes. UA: trace leukocytes, no nitrites.

"Dad Hasn't Been Himself" — The Outpatient Office Visit

"When you're done with residency — unless you go into stroke or neurohospitalist or neuro ICU — your practice flips to about 90% outpatient. This is the kind of case I see all the time now."

Diagnosis: Medication-induced delirium (oxybutynin) superimposed on MCI, with contributing dehydration. Oxybutynin is a potent anticholinergic that crosses the BBB — a Beers Criteria drug. This is the Inouye model in action: high vulnerability (MCI) + minor precipitant (single new drug) = delirium.

Hypoactive presentation is easily mistaken for "worsening dementia" or depression. Do NOT anchor on trace leukocytes in UA — asymptomatic bacteriuria in elderly men with BPH is common.

Management: Discontinue oxybutynin, oral rehydration, follow-up in 48–72 hours. Disposition: safe for home management IF reliable caregiver + identifiable/reversible cause + ability to follow up.

POLL 7
The 78-year-old man in Case 6 developed delirium from a single new medication. According to the Inouye model, which BEST explains this?
High vulnerability (MCI) + minor insult (one new anticholinergic) = delirium. This is the Inouye model's core logic — you don't need a major precipitant when baseline vulnerability is already high.
Session Wrap-Up
  • "Confusion" is a symptom, not a diagnosis — always ask: delirium, encephalopathy, dementia, or psychosis?
  • Inattention is the cardinal feature of delirium
  • Most causes lie outside the brain — "I WATCH DEATH," medications first
  • Confusion + any focal finding = urgent neuroimaging; think stroke, NCSE, encephalitis
  • EEG changes the diagnosis: diffuse slowing, triphasic waves, spatiotemporal evolution, delta brush, PSWCs
  • Treat the cause first; nonpharmacologic management is first-line; benzodiazepines are for withdrawal, not delirium

Open-Recall Case Questions

No multiple choice this time — work the diagnosis out yourself, then reveal.

Case 1: 72F, POD#2 hip arthroplasty, talking to the wall, drowsy → agitated, pulling IV lines. On oxycodone, ondansetron, cefazolin. Diagnosis and top 3 contributors?
Multifactorial delirium — new opioid (oxycodone) in an opioid-naive patient, immobilization/Foley, and sleep deprivation/nighttime disruption. No focal deficits.
Case 2: 55M found down, confused, horizontal nystagmus, wide-based ataxic gait, glucose 60. Diagnosis and imaging findings?
Wernicke encephalopathy. MRI: T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in mammillary bodies, periaqueductal gray, medial thalamus. Treat with thiamine before glucose.
Case 4: 80F, witnessed GTC seizure 4h ago, IV lorazepam given, remains obtunded with subtle rhythmic eye twitching. Diagnosis and next step?
Nonconvulsive status epilepticus. Order continuous EEG — clinical exam alone cannot exclude ongoing electrographic seizures (~48% of treated convulsive SE patients still seizing).
Case 5: 24F, 2-week personality change → paranoia → seizures → orofacial dyskinesias. CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, MRI normal. Diagnosis and required imaging?
Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. Confirm with CSF anti-NMDA receptor antibodies; always get pelvic imaging to look for an ovarian teratoma.
Case 6: 78M, MCI + HTN + BPH, started oxybutynin 5 days ago, now drowsy/inattentive/calling daughter by his deceased wife's name. Trace leukocytes on UA. Diagnosis and disposition?
Medication-induced delirium (oxybutynin, an anticholinergic) superimposed on MCI, with dehydration contributing. Don't anchor on the UA — asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in elderly men with BPH. Stop oxybutynin, hydrate, follow up in 48–72h if a reliable caregiver is present.
